questions.stem: Sperm leaving seminiferous tubules first enter which network before reaching the epididymis?
questions.why: Sperm released into seminiferous tubule lumina pass through straight tubules into the rete testis, an anastomosing network in the mediastinum testis. Efferent ductules subsequently convey them to the epididymis.

notes.B: The ductus deferens receives sperm from the epididymal tail and transports them during emission, downstream of the rete testis.
notes.C: Ejaculatory ducts form from the ductus deferens and seminal vesicle ducts, far downstream of the intratesticular collecting network.
notes.D: The prostatic urethra receives semen from ejaculatory ducts, rather than directly collecting sperm from seminiferous tubules.
notes.E: Seminal vesicles produce accessory gland fluid and do not form the first collecting network for newly produced sperm.

questions.stem: Which duct carries sperm from the rete testis toward the epididymis?
questions.why: Efferent ductules connect the rete testis to the head of the epididymis. Their epithelium absorbs much testicular fluid, concentrating sperm while ciliary and smooth-muscle activity help move them downstream.

notes.A: Ejaculatory ducts deliver semen to the prostatic urethra rather than conveying sperm between rete testis and epididymis.
notes.C: The ductus deferens begins at the epididymal tail, carrying sperm downstream during emission rather than into the epididymal head.
notes.D: Prostatic ducts convey secretions from prostatic glands into the urethra, not sperm from the intratesticular rete.
notes.E: Seminal vesicle ducts contribute accessory gland secretion to ejaculatory ducts rather than connecting the rete testis with the epididymis.

questions.stem: The tunica albuginea of the testis chiefly performs which structural role?
questions.why: The tunica albuginea is a dense fibrous capsule surrounding the testis. Connective-tissue septa extend inward towards the mediastinum, partitioning testicular parenchyma into lobules containing seminiferous tubules and interstitial tissue.

notes.A: Accessory reproductive glands supply seminal fluid, whereas the tunica albuginea provides structural support and organisation of testicular tissue.
notes.B: Germ cells within seminiferous tubules undergo spermatogenesis; the surrounding fibrous capsule does not itself generate sperm cells.
notes.D: Dartos smooth muscle alters scrotal skin tension and surface area, rather than testicular septa arising from the tunica albuginea.
notes.E: Sperm storage occurs principally in the epididymal tail, rather than within the dense connective-tissue capsule of the testis.

questions.stem: Spermatocytes in the adluminal compartment are protected from circulating immune cells by what?
questions.why: Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells divide seminiferous epithelium into basal and adluminal compartments. This blood–testis barrier restricts immune access to developing germ cells and maintains the specialised environment required for meiosis.

notes.A: Leydig-cell testosterone supports spermatogenesis but does not form the physical junctional barrier separating adluminal germ cells from interstitial substances.
notes.B: The pampiniform plexus contributes to testicular heat exchange, rather than forming a selective epithelial barrier within seminiferous tubules.
notes.C: Tunica vaginalis fluid reduces friction around the testis but does not isolate developing spermatocytes within the seminiferous epithelium.
notes.E: Epididymal smooth-muscle contractions help transport sperm downstream and do not establish the intratubular blood–testis barrier.

questions.stem: A selective loss of Sertoli-cell support is expected to impair which process?
questions.why: Sertoli cells provide metabolic substrates, growth factors and structural support to developing germ cells within seminiferous tubules. Loss of this supporting environment impairs germ-cell survival and differentiation, thereby disrupting sperm production.

notes.A: Adrenal steroidogenesis occurs in adrenal cortical cells and is not directly dependent on testicular Sertoli-cell support.
notes.B: Ejaculation depends on coordinated autonomic and somatic neural pathways, rather than the intratubular nourishment function of Sertoli cells.
notes.C: Prostatic epithelial cells produce prostatic fluid under hormonal regulation, rather than receiving direct nutritional support from Sertoli cells.
notes.D: Urethral smooth-muscle tone is regulated largely through autonomic mechanisms and is not the principal target of Sertoli-cell activity.

questions.stem: Which germ cell is formed directly by meiosis I of a primary spermatocyte?
questions.why: Primary spermatocytes undergo the first meiotic division, separating homologous chromosomes to produce secondary spermatocytes. Each resulting cell has a haploid chromosome set, although each chromosome still contains two sister chromatids until meiosis II.

notes.B: Mature spermatozoa arise through subsequent spermiogenesis of spermatids, rather than directly from the first meiotic division.
notes.C: Type A spermatogonia maintain the germ-cell population through mitotic proliferation, preceding entry into meiosis as primary spermatocytes.
notes.D: Round spermatids result from the second meiotic division of secondary spermatocytes, not directly from the first division.
notes.E: Type B spermatogonia are mitotic precursors of primary spermatocytes, rather than haploid products of primary spermatocyte meiosis.

questions.stem: Which cell results immediately from meiosis II in the male germinal epithelium?
questions.why: Secondary spermatocytes undergo meiosis II, separating sister chromatids to form haploid spermatids. These cells subsequently differentiate through spermiogenesis without further cell division, acquiring the specialised morphology of mature spermatozoa.

notes.A: Spermatogonia are mitotically dividing germ-cell precursors that occur before the primary and secondary spermatocyte stages.
notes.C: Primary spermatocytes enter meiosis I and therefore precede the secondary spermatocytes whose second division produces spermatids.
notes.D: Leydig cells are interstitial steroid-producing somatic cells and do not arise from meiotic division of developing male germ cells.
notes.E: Sertoli cells support germ-cell development within seminiferous tubules rather than being products of spermatocyte meiosis.

questions.stem: Which change during spermiogenesis transforms a spermatid without further cell division?
questions.why: Spermiogenesis remodels haploid spermatids into spermatozoa without additional cell division. Golgi-derived vesicles form the acrosome, the nucleus condenses, a flagellum develops and excess cytoplasm is discarded.

notes.A: Spermatocytes are produced earlier from spermatogonial precursors, whereas spermiogenesis remodels already formed haploid spermatids.
notes.B: Meiotic divisions precede spermiogenesis and generate haploid spermatids; differentiation of those spermatids does not require another meiosis.
notes.D: Mitotic spermatogonial proliferation maintains the precursor population before meiosis, rather than transforming spermatids into mature spermatozoa.
notes.E: Primary oocytes are female germ cells and do not arise during male spermatid differentiation in seminiferous tubules.

questions.stem: Which sperm region contains mitochondria arranged to supply motility energy?
questions.why: The sperm midpiece contains a helically arranged mitochondrial sheath surrounding the flagellar apparatus. Mitochondrial oxidative metabolism contributes ATP for motility, alongside glycolysis occurring in other regions of the sperm flagellum.

notes.A: The sperm nucleus contains the compacted paternal genome rather than the mitochondrial sheath supporting flagellar energy metabolism.
notes.B: The acrosomal cap contains specialised material involved in fertilisation, rather than housing the principal organised mitochondrial sheath.
notes.C: The distal flagellar region contributes to propulsion but lacks the mitochondrial sheath characteristic of the midpiece.
notes.E: Centriolar structures help organise the flagellar apparatus, whereas the densely packed mitochondria are arranged along the midpiece.

questions.stem: Which structure contains enzymes used during penetration of the egg investments?
questions.why: The acrosome is a Golgi-derived organelle covering the anterior sperm nucleus. During the acrosome reaction, membrane fusion exposes or releases proteins and enzymes that facilitate sperm interactions with the oocyte's surrounding investments.

notes.A: The midpiece houses mitochondria associated with motility, rather than the specialised enzyme-containing organelle overlying the sperm head.
notes.B: The sperm nucleus carries paternal genetic material and is not the compartment releasing acrosomal enzymes during fertilisation.
notes.C: The epididymal duct provides an environment for sperm maturation, rather than containing the sperm-borne organelle responsible for acrosomal release.
notes.D: Seminal vesicles produce fructose-rich accessory secretion, rather than supplying the acrosomal organelle of individual spermatozoa.

questions.stem: A selective increase in Sertoli-cell inhibin B chiefly feeds back to lower which pituitary hormone?
questions.why: Sertoli cells release inhibin B in association with spermatogenic activity and FSH stimulation. Inhibin B acts on anterior pituitary gonadotrophs to selectively reduce FSH secretion, providing feedback regulation of testicular supporting-cell function.

notes.B: LH secretion is regulated mainly by GnRH and gonadal steroid feedback, whereas inhibin B preferentially suppresses FSH.
notes.C: ACTH controls adrenal glucocorticoid synthesis and is regulated primarily through CRH and cortisol feedback rather than testicular inhibin B.
notes.D: TSH regulates thyroid hormone synthesis and responds to TRH and thyroid hormone feedback, not principally to inhibin B.
notes.E: Growth hormone secretion is governed largely by GHRH, somatostatin and metabolic feedback, rather than selective inhibition by Sertoli-cell inhibin B.

questions.stem: A patient has absent LH signalling but preserved FSH signalling. Which testicular effect is most direct?
questions.why: LH activates receptors on testicular Leydig cells, increasing cAMP-dependent steroidogenic signalling and testosterone production. Loss of LH signalling therefore directly impairs Leydig-cell androgen synthesis even if FSH continues stimulating Sertoli cells.

notes.A: FSH directly stimulates Sertoli-cell function and inhibin B production; its preserved signalling makes Leydig steroidogenesis the more direct defect.
notes.C: Epididymal fluid absorption depends on epithelial transport mechanisms and is not the immediate cellular consequence of absent LH receptor signalling.
notes.D: Acrosomal enzyme release occurs during fertilisation-associated sperm activation, rather than being directly stimulated by circulating LH.
notes.E: Accessory gland secretion depends partly on androgen action, but its composition is a downstream consequence rather than the direct Leydig-cell response.

questions.stem: Why must intratesticular testosterone concentrations remain relatively high?
questions.why: High local testosterone concentrations maintain androgen receptor signalling in testicular supporting cells, especially Sertoli cells. This signalling supports meiotic progression, germ-cell adhesion and spermatid differentiation, and is essential for normal spermatogenesis.

notes.A: Acrosomal discharge occurs after sperm capacitation and appropriate fertilisation-related stimulation, rather than being the principal purpose of high intratesticular testosterone.
notes.B: Urinary continence depends on bladder outlet and sphincter mechanisms, rather than high local androgen concentrations within seminiferous tissue.
notes.D: Seminal fructose is produced largely by seminal vesicles; this accessory gland function does not explain the required high intratesticular androgen concentration.
notes.E: Prostatic contraction during emission depends on autonomic motor activity, rather than the immediate spermatogenic requirement for local testosterone.

questions.stem: How does the pampiniform plexus help sperm production?

options.label: A
options.text: Raises local temperature in the testis

options.label: D
options.text: Cools arterial blood by heat exchange

questions.why: The pampiniform plexus surrounds the testicular artery with relatively cooler returning venous blood. Countercurrent heat transfer cools incoming arterial blood, helping maintain the lower testicular temperature required for efficient spermatogenesis.

notes.A: Raising testicular temperature can impair spermatogenesis, whereas countercurrent exchange generally helps reduce the temperature of arterial inflow.
notes.B: Leydig and Sertoli cells produce testicular regulatory hormones; the pampiniform plexus is a vascular network rather than an endocrine tissue.
notes.C: Sperm are stored principally within the epididymal duct, not within the venous network surrounding the testicular artery.
notes.E: Androgen receptor expression is regulated through cellular mechanisms, while the plexus principally contributes to testicular thermoregulation.

questions.stem: Which scrotal muscle changes testicular position relative to the trunk?
questions.why: The cremaster is striated muscle associated with the spermatic cord that elevates the testis when it contracts. Relaxation permits descent, contributing to positioning of the testis relative to body heat during thermoregulatory responses.

notes.A: Bulbospongiosus contributes to expulsion of semen and urine from the urethra, rather than directly elevating the testis.
notes.B: Ischiocavernosus compresses erectile tissue at the root of the penis and does not directly alter testicular position.
notes.C: The external urethral sphincter provides voluntary urinary outlet control rather than moving the testis towards or away from the trunk.
notes.D: Levator ani supports pelvic organs and contributes to continence, rather than forming the testis-elevating muscle of the spermatic cord.

questions.stem: What is the chief effect of relaxation of dartos smooth muscle in warm conditions?
questions.why: Dartos smooth muscle contracts in cold conditions, wrinkling scrotal skin and reducing exposed surface area. Relaxation in warmth smooths the skin and increases exposed area, facilitating heat loss from the scrotal contents.

notes.B: Reducing scrotal surface area conserves heat and accompanies dartos contraction, rather than relaxation during warm environmental conditions.
notes.C: Testicular elevation is achieved chiefly through cremaster contraction, while dartos relaxation reduces scrotal wrinkling and favours heat dissipation.
notes.D: Pampiniform venous flow supports testicular heat exchange; dartos relaxation does not normally stop this important vascular circulation.
notes.E: Leydig-cell steroid synthesis is principally regulated by LH, rather than being directly accelerated by relaxation of scrotal skin muscle.

questions.stem: Which location is most important for acquisition of sperm motility after testicular production?
questions.why: Sperm leaving the testis are functionally immature and acquire progressive motility competence during passage through the epididymis. Epididymal epithelial secretions and luminal conditions modify their membranes and proteins, preparing them for later capacitation.

notes.A: Seminal vesicles contribute fructose-rich fluid at ejaculation but do not provide the principal site of post-testicular sperm maturation.
notes.C: The prostate contributes seminal fluid and enzymes, rather than providing the prolonged epithelial environment where sperm acquire motility competence.
notes.D: Bulbourethral glands secrete lubricating mucus into the urethra and do not provide the primary maturation pathway for testicular sperm.
notes.E: Ejaculatory ducts convey sperm and glandular secretions towards the urethra, after epididymal maturation has already occurred.

questions.stem: A sperm has reached the uterine tube but cannot undergo the acrosome reaction efficiently. Which preceding process may be defective?
questions.why: Capacitation modifies sperm membrane lipid composition and signalling during exposure to the female reproductive tract or suitable laboratory conditions. These changes promote hyperactivated motility and competence to undergo the acrosome reaction during fertilisation.

notes.A: Spermatogonial mitosis precedes meiosis and sperm differentiation, rather than providing the final functional preparation for the acrosome reaction.
notes.B: Testosterone is produced mainly by Leydig cells, and hepatic testosterone production is not the preceding process enabling acrosomal competence.
notes.D: Seminal vesicles produce accessory secretion rather than storing sperm; functional capacitation occurs after sperm leave the male reproductive tract.
notes.E: Pituitary prolactin has reproductive endocrine roles, but its secretion does not directly remodel the sperm membrane for acrosomal responsiveness.

questions.stem: Which change is characteristic of sperm capacitation?
questions.why: Capacitation involves cholesterol efflux, changes in membrane organisation and removal or modification of inhibitory surface-associated factors acquired in seminal and epididymal fluid. These changes alter sperm signalling and prepare it for fertilisation-associated responses.

notes.A: Sperm form a single acrosome during spermiogenesis; capacitation changes its functional readiness rather than producing an additional acrosomal organelle.
notes.B: Mature sperm do not duplicate their nucleus during capacitation, which primarily modifies cell membranes, motility and intracellular signalling.
notes.C: An intact flagellum is important for reaching the oocyte, and capacitation can promote hyperactivated rather than absent flagellar motility.
notes.E: Meiosis is completed before spermiogenesis and epididymal maturation; capacitation is a functional transformation rather than another chromosome division.

questions.stem: Which accessory gland provides much of the fructose used as an energy substrate by sperm?
questions.why: Seminal vesicles secrete a substantial proportion of seminal plasma, including fructose that can serve as an energy substrate for sperm. Their secretion also contains proteins and other substances contributing to semen composition and function.

notes.A: The prostate supplies citrate, zinc and enzymes, rather than being the principal source of fructose in normal seminal plasma.
notes.B: Bulbourethral glands mainly produce lubricating mucus before ejaculation, rather than providing the major fructose-rich seminal fluid contribution.
notes.C: The epididymal duct supports sperm maturation through specialised epithelial transport and secretion, not the principal fructose-rich accessory gland contribution.
notes.D: Testicular interstitial Leydig cells produce testosterone, whereas seminal fructose is supplied largely by accessory seminal vesicle glands.

questions.stem: Which gland contributes zinc, citrate and proteolytic enzymes to semen?
questions.why: Prostatic epithelial cells secrete citrate, zinc and enzymes including prostate-specific antigen, a protease that cleaves seminal coagulum proteins. These constituents help establish the biochemical environment of semen and permit its liquefaction after ejaculation.

notes.B: Seminal vesicles contribute fructose and coagulum-forming proteins, whereas the prostate provides characteristic zinc, citrate and liquefying proteases.
notes.C: Bulbourethral glands primarily produce lubricating mucus rather than the characteristic citrate-rich secretion containing seminal liquefaction enzymes.
notes.D: The epididymis regulates sperm maturation and storage, rather than supplying the main prostatic biochemical constituents of seminal plasma.
notes.E: Cowper's glands are bulbourethral glands whose ducts convey mucus, rather than the secretory source of prostate-specific antigen and citrate.

questions.stem: A clear lubricating secretion enters the urethra before ejaculation. Which gland provides it?
questions.why: Bulbourethral glands release mucus into the proximal spongy urethra during sexual arousal. This pre-ejaculatory secretion contributes to urethral lubrication and conditions the passage before semen is expelled through it.

notes.A: Seminal vesicles contribute much of the fluid released during emission, rather than being the principal source of early lubricating urethral mucus.
notes.C: The prostate releases fluid containing citrate and proteolytic enzymes during emission, rather than being the principal source of bulbourethral mucus.
notes.D: Seminiferous tubules produce germ cells and testicular fluid, not the mucus released directly into the urethra before ejaculation.
notes.E: Epididymal epithelium supports sperm maturation and storage rather than secreting the characteristic pre-ejaculatory mucus into the urethra.

questions.stem: Which enzyme converts testosterone to a more potent androgen in several target tissues?
questions.why: Five-alpha reductase converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone, which activates androgen receptors with greater potency in several target tissues. DHT is particularly important for external genital development, prostatic growth and selected androgen-dependent hair patterns.

notes.A: Aromatase converts testosterone into estradiol, producing an oestrogen rather than the more potent androgen dihydrotestosterone.
notes.B: Twenty-one hydroxylase participates in adrenal corticosteroid synthesis, rather than reducing testosterone to a more potent androgen in peripheral tissues.
notes.D: Thyroid peroxidase catalyses iodination and coupling during thyroid hormone synthesis, rather than metabolising testosterone to dihydrotestosterone.
notes.E: Aldosterone synthase catalyses late mineralocorticoid biosynthetic reactions, not the peripheral conversion of testosterone into dihydrotestosterone.

questions.stem: Testosterone can support some estrogen-dependent skeletal effects because it can undergo what process?
questions.why: Aromatase converts testosterone into estradiol in various tissues, including bone. Estradiol signalling contributes to epiphyseal maturation, growth-plate fusion and bone maintenance in males as well as females.

notes.A: Cortisol is produced through adrenal glucocorticoid biosynthesis from steroid precursors, rather than by aromatisation of testosterone in skeletal tissue.
notes.B: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid produced in adrenal zona glomerulosa and does not mediate the specified oestrogen-dependent skeletal effects.
notes.C: Thyroxine is an iodinated tyrosine-derived hormone, not a product of testosterone reduction or conversion within skeletal tissue.
notes.E: Adrenaline is a catecholamine derived from tyrosine, rather than an oestrogen formed by metabolic modification of testosterone.

questions.stem: Most circulating testosterone is carried bound to which proteins?
questions.why: Testosterone is lipophilic and circulates largely bound to sex hormone-binding globulin and albumin. SHBG provides high-affinity binding, while albumin binds more weakly; only a small fraction circulates unbound and readily available for receptor interaction.

notes.A: Albumin binds testosterone, but fibrinogen is a clotting protein rather than its principal specialised high-affinity circulating carrier.
notes.B: Transferrin transports iron and ferritin primarily stores it; neither constitutes the principal specialised plasma carrier of testosterone.
notes.C: Haemoglobin and myoglobin bind oxygen in erythrocytes and muscle respectively, rather than transporting most circulating androgen hormone.
notes.D: Thyroglobulin provides the thyroid hormone synthesis scaffold and TBG transports thyroid hormones, rather than forming the principal testosterone-binding pair.

questions.stem: Pelvic parasympathetic activity promotes erection chiefly by increasing what mediator?
questions.why: Pelvic parasympathetic and nitrergic neural activity increases nitric oxide signalling in erectile tissue. Nitric oxide activates soluble guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP and relaxing cavernosal smooth muscle, thereby increasing blood inflow and facilitating venous occlusion.

notes.B: Alpha-1 adrenergic signalling generally contracts cavernosal smooth muscle and favours detumescence rather than initiating parasympathetic erectile relaxation.
notes.C: Endothelin commonly promotes vascular and cavernosal smooth-muscle contraction, rather than providing the principal relaxing mediator during erection.
notes.D: Angiotensin II generally promotes smooth-muscle contraction through AT1 receptor signalling, opposite to the characteristic nitric oxide-mediated erectile relaxation.
notes.E: Vasopressin V1 signalling promotes vasoconstrictor responses rather than the main parasympathetic mechanism increasing blood inflow to erectile tissue.

questions.stem: Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibition facilitates erection by preventing the degradation of what?
questions.why: Phosphodiesterase type 5 hydrolyses cGMP in cavernosal smooth muscle. Inhibiting this enzyme prolongs nitric oxide-dependent cGMP signalling, sustaining relaxation and facilitating the haemodynamic response to appropriate erectile stimulation.

notes.A: Cyclic AMP is degraded by other phosphodiesterase activities and is not the principal substrate selectively targeted by PDE5 inhibitors.
notes.C: Nitric oxide activates soluble guanylyl cyclase upstream of cGMP production; PDE5 inhibition preserves cGMP rather than directly preventing nitric oxide breakdown.
notes.D: Acetylcholine is broken down principally by acetylcholinesterase, whereas phosphodiesterase type 5 acts on the cyclic nucleotide cGMP.
notes.E: Prostaglandin F2alpha is a lipid mediator, not the cyclic nucleotide substrate hydrolysed by phosphodiesterase type 5.

questions.stem: Which autonomic pathway chiefly drives emission of semen into the posterior urethra?
questions.why: Emission depends predominantly on sympathetic activation of smooth muscle in the ductus deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate. Their coordinated contraction moves sperm and accessory gland secretions into the posterior urethra before the expulsive phase.

notes.A: Pelvic parasympathetic pathways principally support erection and related secretory responses, rather than providing the dominant contractile drive for emission.
notes.B: Somatic sensory afferents participate in initiating sexual reflexes but do not directly supply reproductive duct smooth muscle during emission.
notes.D: Vagal pathways regulate many thoracic and abdominal viscera but are not the principal autonomic route controlling male reproductive emission.
notes.E: Enteric neural circuits coordinate gastrointestinal motility and secretion, rather than sympathetic contraction of reproductive ducts and accessory glands.

questions.stem: Rhythmic perineal muscular contractions during expulsion of semen depend mainly on what?
questions.why: During the expulsion phase, sacral somatic motor neurons send signals through pudendal pathways to striated perineal muscles, particularly bulbospongiosus. Rhythmic contraction generates pressure pulses that propel semen through the urethra.

notes.A: Pelvic parasympathetic fibres promote erectile responses but do not provide the principal somatic motor supply to striated expulsive muscles.
notes.B: Vagal preganglionic fibres control selected visceral organs, not the sacral somatic motor pathways coordinating perineal muscle contractions.
notes.C: Cervical sympathetic fibres do not provide direct somatic motor innervation of striated pelvic floor and perineal muscles.
notes.E: Hypophyseal portal vessels transport hypothalamic regulatory hormones rather than conducting rapid motor signals responsible for rhythmic ejaculatory contractions.

questions.stem: A boy has high LH with low testosterone and small testes. Which lesion is most likely?
questions.why: Primary testicular failure reduces testosterone output despite pituitary stimulation. Loss of androgen negative feedback increases LH secretion, producing a hypergonadotropic hypogonadal pattern that distinguishes primary gonadal dysfunction from inadequate hypothalamic or pituitary drive.

notes.A: Primary pituitary failure usually reduces LH secretion, producing low testosterone with inappropriately low or normal gonadotropin concentrations.
notes.B: Hypothalamic GnRH deficiency reduces pituitary gonadotropin stimulation, rather than generating the compensatory LH elevation typical of primary testicular failure.
notes.C: Excess testosterone feedback suppresses LH, which contradicts the combination of low testosterone and elevated LH in this presentation.
notes.D: Isolated adrenal medullary loss affects catecholamine production rather than directly causing failure of testicular steroidogenesis with raised gonadotropins.

questions.stem: Which part of the ovary contains most developing follicles?
questions.why: Developing ovarian follicles occupy the cortical stroma beneath the surface epithelium and tunica albuginea. The central medulla contains relatively loose connective tissue, larger vessels and nerves supplying the ovarian parenchyma.

notes.B: The ovarian medulla contains major vascular and neural structures, whereas most primordial and developing follicles lie within the cortical stroma.
notes.C: Hilar vessels enter or leave the ovary but do not themselves constitute the principal compartment containing developing ovarian follicles.
notes.D: The mesovarium attaches the ovary to the broad ligament and transmits supporting structures, rather than housing the ovarian follicular population.
notes.E: The uterine tube receives the ovulated oocyte but is anatomically separate from the ovarian cortex where follicles develop.

questions.stem: At birth, a normal human primary oocyte is arrested in which meiotic stage?
questions.why: During fetal development, oogonia enter meiosis I and become primary oocytes that arrest in diplotene of prophase I. They remain arrested within follicles until selected oocytes resume meiosis during later reproductive cycles.

notes.A: Metaphase I follows resumption of the first meiotic division and is not the prolonged prenatal arrest stage of primary oocytes.
notes.C: Anaphase I involves separation of homologous chromosomes near completion of the first division, rather than the stage maintained at birth.
notes.D: Meiosis II begins after completion of meiosis I around ovulation, not during the prolonged fetal primary-oocyte arrest.
notes.E: Metaphase II is the normal arrest of the ovulated secondary oocyte, rather than the primary oocyte present at birth.

questions.stem: What meiotic stage characterizes the oocyte normally released at ovulation?
questions.why: The preovulatory LH surge promotes completion of meiosis I, yielding a secondary oocyte and first polar body. The secondary oocyte enters meiosis II and arrests at metaphase II, normally remaining there until fertilisation triggers completion.

notes.A: Prophase I is the prolonged arrest stage of primary oocytes before preovulatory meiotic resumption, rather than the usual ovulated cell stage.
notes.B: Metaphase I is a transient stage preceding formation of the secondary oocyte and first polar body during preovulatory maturation.
notes.D: Anaphase II follows release from metaphase II arrest after activation of the secondary oocyte, normally triggered by fertilisation.
notes.E: Telophase II occurs during completion of the second meiotic division, which normally follows fertilisation rather than preceding ovulation.

questions.stem: After sperm entry, what event allows the secondary oocyte to form the mature ovum?
questions.why: Sperm–oocyte fusion normally initiates intracellular calcium oscillations that release the secondary oocyte from metaphase II arrest. Completion of meiosis II separates sister chromatids and extrudes the second polar body, producing the mature female gamete.

notes.A: Mitosis preserves chromosome number and is not the division completing maturation of the metaphase II-arrested secondary oocyte.
notes.B: Meiosis I has usually finished before ovulation, producing the secondary oocyte and first polar body, rather than occurring after sperm entry.
notes.C: Oogonia are proliferative germ-cell precursors of fetal development; sperm entry does not normally generate another oogonium.
notes.E: Prophase I precedes the first meiotic division, whereas fertilisation-associated activation allows the arrested secondary oocyte to proceed forward through meiosis II.

questions.stem: Why does human oogenesis generate one large gamete and small polar bodies?
questions.why: Oocyte meiotic divisions segregate chromosomes while partitioning cytoplasm asymmetrically. Small polar bodies receive chromosome sets but little cytoplasm, preserving organelles, maternal RNA and other resources within the large gamete needed to support early embryonic development.

notes.A: Equal cytoplasmic division would distribute cellular resources among multiple similar-sized products rather than preserving most cytoplasm within one large oocyte.
notes.B: Repeated mitosis maintains or expands precursor cells but cannot explain haploid gamete formation with chromosome-containing polar bodies.
notes.C: Fusion of two oocytes does not generate normal polar bodies; these result from asymmetric cytokinesis during the oocyte's meiotic divisions.
notes.D: Chromosome segregation must occur correctly to produce haploid products; unequal cytoplasmic partitioning does not imply failure of chromosome separation.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a primordial follicle from a growing primary follicle?
questions.why: A primordial follicle contains a prophase I-arrested primary oocyte surrounded by a single layer of flattened pregranulosa cells. During activation, these cells become cuboidal and proliferate as the follicle enters the growing primary stage.

notes.B: A large antrum develops during later follicular growth and is absent from both primordial and early primary follicles.
notes.C: Luteinisation is associated with periovulatory transformation of follicular cells, rather than being a defining feature of a resting primordial follicle.
notes.D: The zona pellucida develops around the growing oocyte; complete loss of this structure is not the distinguishing primordial follicle feature.
notes.E: The corpus luteum forms from the ruptured follicle after ovulation, rather than representing the earliest resting follicular stage.

questions.stem: Which structure appears as fluid spaces merge during antral follicle growth?
questions.why: As granulosa cells proliferate and follicular fluid accumulates, small extracellular fluid spaces merge into a larger antrum. This cavity characterises antral follicles and enlarges considerably during selection and maturation of the dominant follicle.

notes.A: The corpus albicans is a fibrous remnant of a regressed corpus luteum rather than the fluid-filled cavity of a growing follicle.
notes.C: The zona reticularis is an adrenal cortical steroidogenic layer and does not form within an ovarian antral follicle.
notes.D: The ovarian medulla is a central vascular stromal region, rather than a cavity produced by accumulation of follicular fluid.
notes.E: The uterine tube isthmus is a narrow muscular segment of the oviduct, not a structure appearing within the growing ovarian follicle.

questions.stem: Atresia of non-dominant follicles during each cycle explains which observation?
questions.why: Several follicles may grow during a menstrual cycle, but one usually becomes dominant through enhanced responsiveness and favourable hormonal conditions. Declining FSH availability contributes to regression of other follicles through atresia, so usually only one ovulates.

notes.A: Most recruited follicles undergo atresia rather than proceeding to ovulation, making simultaneous ovulation of every recruited follicle unusual.
notes.B: The great majority of primordial follicles never reach ovulation; many undergo atresia during reproductive life or remain dormant.
notes.D: Luteal cells develop from periovulatory follicular cells after the antral follicle has matured, not before the antral stage.
notes.E: Secondary oocytes are normally formed near ovulation after puberty, whereas prepubertal follicles generally contain arrested primary oocytes.

questions.stem: In the two-cell model, LH stimulates theca cells chiefly to generate which substrate?
questions.why: LH stimulates theca interna cells to synthesise androgen precursors from cholesterol. These androgens diffuse into neighbouring granulosa cells, where FSH-regulated aromatase converts them into oestrogens, demonstrating cooperation between two follicular cell types.

notes.A: Progesterone becomes a major luteal steroid after ovulation, but the key thecal substrate for granulosa aromatase is androgen.
notes.B: Prolactin is produced principally by anterior pituitary lactotrophs, rather than being the follicular steroid substrate supplied by theca cells.
notes.C: Oxytocin is a hypothalamic peptide hormone released from the posterior pituitary, rather than a theca-derived aromatase substrate.
notes.E: Inhibin is a granulosa-associated regulatory protein that suppresses FSH and cannot serve as a steroid substrate for aromatase.

questions.stem: FSH acts on granulosa cells to increase estradiol primarily through which enzyme?
questions.why: FSH activates granulosa-cell signalling that increases aromatase expression and activity. Aromatase converts theca-derived androgen precursors into oestrogens, including estradiol, supporting follicular maturation and the progressive rise in circulating oestrogen during the follicular phase.

notes.A: Five-alpha reductase converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone rather than catalysing oestrogen formation in ovarian granulosa cells.
notes.B: Twenty-one hydroxylase contributes to adrenal glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid biosynthesis, rather than converting follicular androgens into oestrogens.
notes.C: Thyroid peroxidase catalyses iodination reactions within thyroid follicles, not ovarian conversion of androgen precursors into estradiol.
notes.D: Renin initiates angiotensin peptide formation by cleaving angiotensinogen and does not catalyse ovarian steroid aromatisation.

questions.stem: Which ovarian phase varies most between women and between cycles?
questions.why: The follicular phase varies in length because the timing of follicular recruitment, selection and maturation differs between cycles. The postovulatory luteal phase is generally more consistent, although its duration is not completely fixed.

notes.B: The luteal phase usually varies less than the follicular phase because corpus luteum function has a relatively constrained duration without pregnancy.
notes.C: Corpus luteum lifespan influences luteal-phase duration, but variability in time to ovulation usually accounts for more cycle-length variation.
notes.D: The progesterone-dominant postovulatory phase corresponds to the luteal phase and is generally less variable than the preceding follicular interval.
notes.E: The endometrial secretory phase follows ovulation and largely parallels luteal progesterone exposure, rather than being the main variable preovulatory interval.

questions.stem: Sustained high estradiol before ovulation changes hypothalamic-pituitary feedback in what direction?
questions.why: Sustained high estradiol from the dominant follicle changes hypothalamic–pituitary regulation from predominantly negative to positive feedback. Increased gonadotropin drive and pituitary responsiveness generate the preovulatory LH surge, which initiates final oocyte maturation and follicular rupture.

notes.A: Moderate estradiol concentrations ordinarily exert negative feedback, but sustained high preovulatory estradiol promotes rather than prevents the LH surge.
notes.C: The preovulatory response involves increased pituitary responsiveness to GnRH rather than complete loss of its receptors and gonadotropin stimulation.
notes.D: FSH may exhibit a smaller midcycle surge, so complete suppression of follicular FSH is not the defining positive-feedback response.
notes.E: Ovarian LH receptors participate in the response to the gonadotropin surge; their inactivation would oppose normal ovulatory events.

questions.stem: Which pituitary event most directly triggers rupture of the mature follicle?
questions.why: The LH surge promotes ovulation and oocyte maturation.

questions.stem: What mainly maintains corpus luteum activity in an early established pregnancy?
questions.why: Trophoblastic hCG rescues the corpus luteum from regression.

questions.stem: If fertilization does not occur, regression of the corpus luteum causes what?
questions.why: Loss of luteal hormones precipitates endometrial breakdown and menstruation.

questions.stem: Which endometrial layer is shed during normal menstruation?
questions.why: Most of the functional endometrial layer is shed; the basal layer remains.

questions.stem: Which arteries are particularly involved in ischaemic breakdown of the menstrual endometrium?
questions.why: Constriction of spiral arteries supplying the functionalis contributes to menstruation.

questions.stem: Which ovarian hormone predominantly drives endometrial proliferation before ovulation?
questions.why: Estradiol promotes endometrial repair and proliferation in the follicular phase.

questions.stem: Why do endometrial glands become coiled and secretory after ovulation?
questions.why: Luteal progesterone converts proliferative endometrium into a secretory lining.

questions.stem: Why does normal menstrual blood often fail to clot despite uterine bleeding?
questions.why: Endometrial fibrinolytic activity breaks down fibrin in menstrual discharge.

questions.stem: Which change around ovulation most facilitates sperm passage through the cervix?
questions.why: Oestrogen produces abundant thin elastic cervical mucus around ovulation.

questions.stem: After ovulation, progesterone causes which change in cervical secretions?
questions.why: Progesterone makes cervical mucus thick and less favorable to sperm transport.

questions.stem: A sustained rise in basal body temperature after ovulation is mainly due to which hormone?
questions.why: Progesterone exerts a thermogenic effect in the luteal phase.

questions.stem: Which ovarian steroid stimulates growth of mammary ducts at puberty?
questions.why: Estrogens promote ductal development, while progesterone supports lobuloalveolar differentiation.

questions.stem: Which hormone particularly supports secretory development of mammary alveoli?
questions.why: Progesterone promotes lobuloalveolar maturation during the reproductive cycle and pregnancy.

questions.stem: What ovarian hormone strongly inhibits pituitary FSH release independently of much LH feedback?
questions.why: Granulosa-derived inhibin selectively suppresses FSH secretion.

questions.stem: A woman training intensively has amenorrhoea and low gonadotropins. What mechanism best explains it?
questions.why: Energy deficit and stress can suppress GnRH pulsatility and produce hypothalamic amenorrhoea.

questions.stem: Why can hyperprolactinaemia cause infertility in a woman with otherwise normal ovaries?
questions.why: Elevated prolactin suppresses GnRH and ovulatory gonadotropin secretion.

questions.stem: Painful menstrual cramping is strongly associated with which uterine mediator?
questions.why: Endometrial prostaglandins promote myometrial contractions and menstrual pain.

questions.stem: Why does FSH commonly rise markedly after menopause?
questions.why: Follicle depletion reduces estrogen and inhibin feedback, permitting increased FSH secretion.

questions.stem: A capacitated sperm binds the zona pellucida but cannot release acrosomal contents. Which step fails?
questions.why: The acrosome reaction releases enzymes that facilitate penetration of the zona pellucida.

questions.stem: Which sperm change particularly helps it traverse the cumulus cell layer around the oocyte?
questions.why: Capacitated sperm display vigorous hyperactivated motility for penetration of egg investments.

questions.stem: The oocyte's cortical granules release their contents after sperm entry mainly to prevent what?

options.label: E
options.text: Migration of the first polar body

questions.why: The cortical reaction modifies the zona pellucida and prevents polyspermy.

questions.stem: What intracellular signal helps activate the secondary oocyte after sperm-egg fusion?
questions.why: Sperm entry triggers calcium oscillations that promote oocyte activation and meiosis completion.

questions.stem: Which stage forms as cleavage produces a compact ball of blastomeres before a fluid cavity appears?
questions.why: The morula is a solid mass of cells that develops before the fluid-filled blastocyst.

questions.stem: In a blastocyst, which cell population mainly gives rise to the embryo proper?
questions.why: The embryoblast or inner cell mass develops into the embryo.

questions.stem: Which outer trophoblast layer actively invades maternal endometrium during implantation?
questions.why: Invasive syncytiotrophoblast penetrates decidual tissue to establish implantation.

questions.stem: Why do chorionic villi become increasingly effective sites of exchange during development?
questions.why: Developing fetal capillaries approach maternal blood spaces across the placental barrier.

questions.stem: Which exchange normally crosses the placental membrane by facilitated transport rather than simple lipid diffusion?
questions.why: Glucose enters fetal circulation largely through placental glucose transporters such as GLUT1.

questions.stem: Which maternal antibody class normally crosses the placenta most efficiently?
questions.why: Fc receptor-mediated transfer of IgG provides passive fetal immunity.

questions.stem: How are the maternal and fetal circulations normally related inside a placental villus?
questions.why: Maternal blood bathes villi while fetal blood remains within villous capillaries.

questions.stem: Which placental cell layer produces most circulating maternal hCG?
questions.why: Syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG into maternal blood.

questions.stem: In later pregnancy, placental lactogen helps spare maternal glucose for the fetus by doing what?
questions.why: Human placental lactogen promotes maternal insulin resistance and mobilization of fat.

questions.stem: Which placental steroid is particularly important for maintaining uterine quiescence?
questions.why: Progesterone reduces myometrial excitability during much of gestation.

questions.stem: Near term, increased myometrial responsiveness to oxytocin is largely aided by what?
questions.why: More oxytocin receptors and gap junctions promote coordinated strong uterine contractions.

questions.stem: Why can maternal circulating insulin rise during late normal pregnancy?

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of maternal pancreatic beta cells

questions.why: Maternal beta cells compensate for placental-hormone-induced insulin resistance.

questions.stem: Why does maternal arterial carbon dioxide tension normally fall during pregnancy?
questions.why: Progesterone increases respiratory drive, producing mild compensated respiratory alkalosis.

questions.stem: Why does maternal cardiac output normally increase during pregnancy?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower blood volume and heart rate

options.label: C
options.text: Higher stroke volume and heart rate

questions.why: Plasma volume, heart rate and stroke volume rise to meet uteroplacental demands.

questions.stem: Why may maternal haematocrit fall during normal pregnancy despite a rise in red-cell mass?

options.label: B
options.text: Increased destruction of maternal red cells

options.label: C
options.text: Reduced erythrocyte survival in the fetus

questions.why: Maternal plasma volume expands more than red-cell mass, producing physiological haemodilution.

questions.stem: Cervical pressure from the fetal head reinforces uterine contractions through which reflex?
questions.why: Cervical stretch increases oxytocin release through the Ferguson positive feedback reflex.

questions.stem: Which mediator is especially involved in cervical softening and ripening near delivery?
questions.why: Prostaglandin E2 promotes cervical remodeling and participates in labour.

questions.stem: Increasing gap junctions between myometrial cells near term have what functional consequence?

options.label: C
options.text: Loss of all uterine electrical coupling

questions.why: Gap junctions electrically couple myometrial cells to promote synchronized labour.

questions.stem: Which stimulus provides a mechanical contribution to the initiation and reinforcement of labour?

options.label: C
options.text: Distension of the uterus and cervix

questions.why: Stretch and cervical pressure increase contractility and oxytocin-related feedback.

questions.stem: What principally distinguishes prolactin from oxytocin in breastfeeding?
questions.why: Prolactin drives milk production, while oxytocin drives ejection.

questions.stem: A mother has adequate prolactin but poor milk removal from the breast. What can eventually happen?
questions.why: Milk accumulation locally inhibits continued milk production; regular removal helps sustain supply.

questions.stem: What term describes the established phase of lactation maintained by ongoing milk removal?
questions.why: After the onset of copious secretion, established milk production depends on continued emptying and local milk-demand signals.

questions.stem: Why do milk volumes rise sharply after placental delivery?
questions.why: Placental progesterone withdrawal permits the onset of copious lactogenesis.

questions.stem: Frequent exclusive suckling can delay ovulation by reducing which hypothalamic signal?
questions.why: Lactational amenorrhoea involves suppression of GnRH pulsatility and gonadotropin release.

questions.stem: Which sensory event starts the neuroendocrine milk-ejection reflex?
questions.why: Suckling activates nipple afferents that drive hypothalamic oxytocin release.

questions.stem: Which event is most likely to acutely interrupt milk let-down despite adequate milk production?
questions.why: Stress can impair the centrally mediated oxytocin let-down reflex even when milk is present.

questions.stem: The lobuloalveolar structures of the breast grow extensively during pregnancy under which hormones?
questions.why: Estrogen supports ducts, and progesterone supports lobuloalveolar development.

questions.stem: What fetal vessel is most directly surrounded by maternal blood in the placental intervillous space?
questions.why: The trophoblastic placental barrier separates maternal intervillous blood from fetal villous capillaries.

questions.stem: Maternal-fetal transfer of oxygen is mainly driven by what?
questions.why: Oxygen diffuses down its partial-pressure gradient across the placenta.

questions.stem: Which vessel carries comparatively oxygenated blood from the placenta toward the fetal liver?
questions.why: One umbilical vein returns oxygenated placental blood to the fetus.

questions.stem: Which vessels convey fetal blood toward the placenta for oxygenation?
questions.why: Paired umbilical arteries return comparatively deoxygenated blood to the placenta.

questions.stem: The ductus venosus directs part of umbilical venous blood into which vessel?
questions.why: The ductus venosus bypasses part of the liver and joins the inferior vena cava.

questions.stem: What is the main direction of blood movement through the fetal foramen ovale?
questions.why: The foramen ovale permits right-to-left atrial shunting before birth.

questions.stem: Which fetal channel connects the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta?
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus shunts blood away from high-resistance fetal lungs.

questions.stem: Why is pulmonary blood flow relatively low in the fetus?
questions.why: Fluid-filled, unventilated fetal lungs maintain high pulmonary vascular resistance.

questions.stem: What makes placental circulation a major low-resistance component of fetal systemic flow?

options.label: C
options.text: Complete lack of fetal cardiac output

questions.why: The placental circulation forms a low-resistance pathway in fetal circulation.

questions.stem: Why is oxygenated blood from the ductus venosus preferentially directed toward the fetal brain and heart?

options.label: C
options.text: Shunting from aorta to vena cava

questions.why: Streaming of inferior vena caval blood across the foramen ovale favors supply to the left heart.

questions.stem: Why do fetal ventricles function more in parallel than in series?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the left ventricle pumps blood

options.label: C
options.text: Only the right ventricle pumps blood

options.label: D
options.text: All blood must cross the lungs

questions.why: Fetal shunts distribute combined ventricular output to the systemic and placental circulations.

questions.stem: Which fetal chamber pumps most of its output into the ductus arteriosus?
questions.why: High pulmonary resistance diverts much right ventricular output through the ductus arteriosus.

questions.stem: The first effective breaths rapidly lower pulmonary vascular resistance mainly through what?
questions.why: Aeration and higher alveolar oxygen dilate pulmonary vessels.

questions.stem: Clamping the umbilical cord normally causes which immediate systemic change?
questions.why: Removal of low-resistance placental circulation raises systemic vascular resistance.

questions.stem: Functional closure of the foramen ovale follows which pressure relationship?
questions.why: Increased pulmonary venous return raises left atrial pressure and opposes right-to-left shunting.

questions.stem: Why does the ductus arteriosus constrict after a healthy term birth?
questions.why: Increased arterial oxygen and falling prostaglandins favor ductal constriction.

questions.stem: Which adult anatomical remnant derives from the ductus arteriosus?
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.stem: Which adult structure marks the closed fetal foramen ovale?
questions.why: Fusion of the atrial septal flap leaves the fossa ovalis.

questions.stem: Which adult remnant corresponds to the former ductus venosus?
questions.why: The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum in the liver.

questions.stem: After birth, the umbilical vein normally forms which hepatic structure?
questions.why: The remnant of the left umbilical vein is the round ligament of the liver.

questions.stem: Premature neonates are especially vulnerable to alveolar collapse mainly because of low levels of what?
questions.why: Type II pneumocyte surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension and prevents atelectasis.

questions.stem: Which lung cell is responsible for synthesis and secretion of pulmonary surfactant?
questions.why: Type II alveolar cells produce surfactant.

questions.stem: Successful clearance of fetal lung liquid at birth relies importantly on increased what?
questions.why: Birth-related epithelial sodium transport helps remove fluid from the airspaces.

questions.stem: What is the principal effect of pulmonary surfactant during the newborn's first breaths?
questions.why: Surfactant reduces the pressure needed to inflate small alveoli.

questions.stem: Why are preterm babies prone to hypoglycaemia shortly after birth?
questions.why: Limited glycogen and fat stores plus immature glucose production increase vulnerability.

questions.stem: Newborn infants generate heat without shivering predominantly by oxidizing what tissue?
questions.why: Brown fat supports nonshivering thermogenesis through mitochondrial uncoupling.

questions.stem: Which mitochondrial protein enables heat generation in neonatal brown adipose tissue?
questions.why: UCP1 dissipates the proton gradient as heat instead of conserving it as ATP.

questions.stem: Physiological neonatal jaundice is partly related to immaturity of which liver process?
questions.why: Immature UGT-mediated conjugation reduces bilirubin clearance in the newborn.

questions.stem: Why is vitamin K prophylaxis important soon after birth?

options.label: A
options.text: Excess vitamin K from placental blood

options.label: E
options.text: Low stores and limited gut vitamin K

questions.why: Neonates have limited vitamin K reserves and immature intestinal flora.

questions.stem: Which renal feature makes young neonates more vulnerable to fluid imbalance?

options.label: A
options.text: Low GFR and limited concentrating ability

questions.why: Immature filtration and tubular function limit neonatal water and solute regulation.

questions.stem: Why is severe neonatal bradycardia especially likely to depress cardiac output?

options.label: A
options.text: Excess ability to increase stroke volume

options.label: B
options.text: Limited ability to raise stroke volume

questions.why: The neonatal heart is relatively heart-rate dependent because stroke volume reserve is limited.

questions.stem: Fetal haemoglobin has reduced affinity for which red-cell regulator compared with adult Hb?
questions.why: HbF binds 2,3-BPG less strongly, helping it acquire oxygen at placental tensions.

questions.stem: What happens to the predominant haemoglobin composition after the neonatal period?
questions.why: Gamma-chain synthesis declines while beta-chain-containing adult Hb rises after birth.

questions.stem: A newborn with persistent high pulmonary resistance continues a right-to-left ductal shunt. Which condition does this describe?
questions.why: Persistent pulmonary hypertension maintains high PVR and can preserve fetal right-to-left shunting.

questions.stem: Which clinical change most often marks the beginning of normal male puberty?
questions.why: Testicular enlargement is typically the earliest clear sign of male puberty.

questions.stem: Kisspeptin signalling at puberty chiefly increases secretion of which hypothalamic hormone?
questions.why: Kisspeptin activates GnRH neurons and helps initiate pulsatile gonadotropin secretion.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy has no increase in testicular size. This most strongly suggests what?
questions.why: Lack of testicular enlargement by 14 warrants evaluation for delayed puberty.

questions.stem: A genetic male with deficient five-alpha reductase may develop ambiguous external genitalia because which hormone is deficient locally?
questions.why: DHT supports development of male external genitalia during fetal life.

questions.stem: Which androgen is particularly important for development of the male internal Wolffian ducts?
questions.why: Testosterone supports Wolffian duct derivatives, while DHT chiefly masculinizes external genitalia.

questions.stem: What mechanical process helps maintain an erection after cavernosal smooth muscle relaxes?
questions.why: Expanding sinusoids compress emissary veins against the tunica albuginea.

questions.stem: Increased sympathetic alpha-adrenergic activity terminates erection primarily by what?
questions.why: Alpha-adrenergic contraction reduces arterial inflow and restores venous drainage.

questions.stem: A boy with severe testosterone deficiency before puberty may develop which finding?
questions.why: Without adequate testosterone the expected pubertal masculine changes are blunted.

questions.stem: Which event is commonly the first visible sign of female puberty?
questions.why: Thelarche generally precedes pubic hair maturation and menarche.

questions.stem: Pulsatile rather than continuous GnRH signalling is physiologically necessary mainly to maintain what?
questions.why: Pulsatile GnRH sustains gonadotropin secretion; continuous exposure desensitizes the system.

questions.stem: What is the conventional clinical definition of natural menopause?
questions.why: Natural menopause is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhoea without another cause.

questions.stem: A menopausal woman's vasomotor hot flushes are principally associated with what endocrine transition?

options.label: A
options.text: Rapid rise in corpus luteum progesterone

questions.why: Follicle depletion lowers estrogen and affects central temperature regulation.

questions.stem: Why does ovulation cease in natural menopause despite elevated FSH?
questions.why: Loss of the follicular pool prevents effective ovarian response to high gonadotropins.

questions.stem: Which sequence represents the conventional four-phase human sexual response model?
questions.why: The EPOR model comprises excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution.

questions.stem: Which autonomic mechanism contributes importantly to genital vasocongestion during arousal?
questions.why: Parasympathetic vasodilatation increases genital blood flow during arousal.

questions.stem: Vaginal lubrication during arousal arises substantially from which process?
questions.why: Increased genital blood flow causes plasma transudation across vaginal mucosa.

questions.stem: The resolution phase of the sexual response cycle is best characterized by what?

options.label: B
options.text: Return of genital blood flow toward baseline

questions.why: Resolution follows orgasm or cessation of stimulation with return toward resting physiology.
